chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Abd al-Rahman from Hammad from Hariz from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by Ka'b ibn Ujrah al-Ansari, and lice were falling from his head. He said: 'Do the insects of your head annoy you?' He said: 'Yes.'
Then this verse was revealed: 'So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [from fasting] must offer a ransom of fasting [three days] or charity or a sacrifice.'

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ordered him, so he shaved his head. He made upon him fasting for three days, and charity for six poor people, two mudds for each poor person, and the sacrifice is one sheep.

key_terms.فِدْيَةٌ: Ransom or expiation offered in lieu of an obligation
key_terms.مُدَّانِ: Two measures of mudd (a unit of volume)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation (kaffarah) for breaking fast due to illness or head lice according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahar establishes the jurisprudential distinction between elective options (ikhtiyar) and mandatory sequences (iltizam) in Quranic exegesis, using the case of Ka'b ibn Ujrah's lice infestation as the primary precedent. It highlights the Shia scholarly method of deriving legal flexibility from the linguistic structure of the verse, affirming that the fidyah for illness is a choice among fasting, charity, or sacrifice rather than a cumulative obligation.
